components.description: Why prior token merging fails with fast attention, and the ToMA design built to fix it

nodes.name: Quadratic attention bottlenecks diffusion
nodes.description: Self-attention in diffusion transformers (U-ViT, DiT) has quadratic complexity in token count, which causes latency across denoising steps.

nodes.name: Prior merging uses GPU-inefficient ops
nodes.description: Prior token-reduction methods for diffusion (ToMeSD, Token Pruning, ToFu) rely on GPU-inefficient primitives such as sorting and scattered memory writes.

nodes.name: Merge overhead negates speedups with fast attention
nodes.description: When paired with optimized attention such as FlashAttention in diffusers, the overhead of earlier merging logic dominates computation time and prevents practical speedups.

nodes.name: Facility location selects destination tokens
nodes.description: ToMA formulates destination-token selection as a submodular optimization problem solved with a GPU-optimized facility location algorithm, choosing a diverse and representative token set.

nodes.name: Merge and unmerge as attention-like linear maps
nodes.description: ToMA merges non-destination tokens into destinations via an attention-like linear transformation and unmerges them via an inverse transformation, using GPU-friendly matrix multiplications.

nodes.name: Transpose approximates pseudo-inverse
nodes.description: Because facility-location destinations cover largely disjoint source sets and low attention temperature sharpens the softmax, the merge matrix rows are near-orthonormal, so the transpose approximates the pseudo-inverse and is used as the default unmerge.

nodes.name: Locality enables tile-parallel merging
nodes.description: Latent tokens exhibit spatial coherence, so merging can run in parallel within non-overlapping local tiles.

nodes.name: Destinations persist across steps and layers
nodes.description: Over a 10-step window, more than half of destination tokens are reused, so ToMA reuses destination sets and linear merge/unmerge weights across consecutive steps and layers to amortize overhead.

nodes.name: ToMA speeds up SDXL and Flux
nodes.description: ToMA reduces total generation time by 24% for SDXL-base and 23% for Flux.1-dev with negligible quality change (DINO delta < 0.07).

nodes.name: Tile vs stripe vs once trade-offs
nodes.description: ToMAtile gives the best DINO score but is slowed by memory copying, ToMAstripe is faster but slightly lower quality, and ToMAonce is fastest but has the worst quality; ToMA's default locality-aware variant balances them with up to 24% speedup.

nodes.name: ToMA fastest among token-reduction baselines
nodes.description: On SDXL ToMA achieves the fastest generation time (up to 28.5% improvement) with competitive quality, while ToMe is slower due to sorting and ToFu shows unstable quality.

isolated_nodes.name: Flux excludes stripe merging
isolated_nodes.description: Stripe-based merging is incompatible with the rotary positional embedding (RoPE) used in Flux, so only ToMA and ToMAtile are evaluated on it.

isolated_nodes.name: ToMA is training-free
isolated_nodes.description: ToMA is a training-free, plug-and-play framework that needs no auxiliary modules, unlike learned token reduction methods such as DynamicViT and A-ViT.

isolated_nodes.name: ToFu merges or prunes per layer
isolated_nodes.description: ToFu decides per layer whether to merge or prune tokens based on a linearity test.

isolated_nodes.name: Submodularity gives coverage guarantee
isolated_nodes.description: Submodular optimization provides theoretical guarantees that ToMA's token selection approximates optimal coverage.

structural_reasoning: Problem (quadratic attention, inefficient prior merging) motivates the GPU-aligned ToMA design, whose components lead to the speedup results and benchmark comparison.
